Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yes, of course. So that was a really interesting story. And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And do you still believe that this is true? Do you still believe that like at the end, it doesn't really matter?

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

Zhuang Liu: Yep. so I will first talk a little bit about the context, the background. so over years, people have been-- So this, this, this paper is more vision-focused. over years, people have been developing larger and larger datasets and, from more and more diverse sources. And, it's, it's, it was kind of tempting to make the assumption that we are good, already good with datasets because it's really all the things you can get from internet, from these datasets. but in some of our initial experiments, we found that these datasets are nothing, still nothing like each other.

And how, how do we measure this? We, we designed a very dumb experiment that's, doesn't make sense at all as a, as a, like, a deep learning training, program. What we did is this. given three very large scale computer vision datasets, we train and classify neural network to classify, to classify which, which dataset a given particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem, it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. it's a multi-ca- multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly non-- very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, up to, more, higher than 80% accuracy when, when you have three datasets.

So the random guessing accuracy will be 33%, but in fact, the model can be, much better, than that. So this say, this means to a model, these datasets still, are still very, very different. It has very clear cues for the model to tell which dataset this, this image comes from. Of course, we are doing this on held out validation sets. We are not, like, predicting the training, training images. but still, this has been surprisingly high, surprisingly accurate, and, that like prompts us to reflect, are we really su- have we, we really been successful in curating a large scale, all-encompassing dataset, at least in computer vision domain? But that doesn't mean you can just remove it and everything works. The replacement still has to do something useful. So the question is, what function does this component actually serve, and is there a simpler way to achieve that?

That's also how I think about the ConvNeXt work. We inherited a lot of design choices, and once the whole system works well, people tend to keep those choices. It becomes hard to tell which ones are necessary and which ones are just one reasonable solution.

I still think residual connections, for example, are very important. But even there, how exactly you connect the layers is something you can explore. And you have to tune the resulting model properly. Otherwise, you might conclude that a component is essential just because the training recipe was developed around it. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think probably many of them are. Normalization was a particularly interesting example because people treated it almost as a necessary condition for training deep transformers, but once you understand what role it is playing—keeping the activations in a reasonable range—you may be able to achieve that with a much simpler mechanism, like dynamic tanh.

I would also question the exact choice of activation functions, the precise placement of feed-forward layers, positional encodings, and even some aspects of attention. I don’t mean that all of these can simply be removed without consequence. Usually they are solving a real optimization or representation problem. But the particular solution we inherited may be historical: it worked early, the ecosystem optimized around it, and then it became the default.

Residual connections may be closer to something genuinely fundamental, because they make very deep networks trainable, but even there, the exact way layers are connected is still an active design space. So my general view is that we should distinguish the function a component provides from its current implementation. The function may be essential, while the familiar component itself may not be.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, so first, a small clarification on that paper, because I think it's easy to over-read. our point was not really that normalization is useless or that people should go, remove all the norm layers tomorrow. what, what started the project was we plotted what LayerNorm actually does to the activations in a trained transformer, and the input-output mapping just looks like a tanh curve. It's, it's squashing the extreme values, and for most of the tokens, it's almost linear. So then the question becomes, is the thing we need the statistics, the computing mean and variance across the token, or is it just the squashing? And it turns out, at least in the settings we tried, it's mostly the squashing. So you can replace it with a, a element-wise tanh with a learnable scale, and you, you stay on the same frontier. So again, it's a lesson about, about what the component is actually doing rather than, than a, a replacement I'm pushing on everyone. Yeah.

but to your question, yeah, I think there are, there are quite a few. I mean, the, the test I would use is, can you swap it out or remove it, and with, with proper tuning of both sides, do you stay on that same accuracy-efficiency curve? If yes, then it, it was probably a historical accident, or at least, it was one, one reasonable choice among many that got frozen because everybody copied the same codebase.

So, dropout is, is maybe the, the clearest case that already happened, right? Like, dropout was, was considered essential. Every paper had dropout. And then at some point, we, we moved to, large data, one epoch regimes, and it just, quietly disappeared. Nobody wrote a paper saying dropout is dead. It just, it just stopped being in the configs. So I, I think that's a, a good example that the essentialness was, was conditional on the data regime, not on anything fundamental.

Other candidates, I would say the, the specific numbers. Like the four-times expansion ratio in the feedforward layer, the, the number of heads, head dimension of 64, patch size 16 and 224 resolution in vision. these are, these are all just, inherited. I don't think anybody has a principled derivation for four. it's, it's probably fine, it's probably near the frontier, but it's, it's not essential. and then cosine learning rate schedule with, with linear warmup, I, I think that one is, is also somewhat accidental. people are now finding that, constant plus, plus a decay at the end works just as well and is much more convenient if you don't know your token budget in advance.

The bigger ones, that I'm, I'm less sure about, but I suspect, tokenization. BPE is, is very clearly a, an engineering compromise, right? It's, it's there because we can't afford byte-level or character-level compute. And, and a lot of the weird failures, like counting letters, arithmetic, come from that choice. So that one, I, I would, I'd bet that's an accident that we, we will look back on. and the optimizer, Adam with those particular betas. people are now, showing Muon and other things work, so, so that's clearly not a unique point.

what I don't think is accidental, the residual connection. I, I really think that one is fundamental, in, in the sense that it defines the, the optimization landscape and lets you scale depth at all. and, and the attention mechanism, or, or some mechanism for token mixing with, with content-dependent routing. the specific softmax form, maybe. But, the fact that you need, something that lets tokens talk to each other in a, a data-dependent way, I, I think that's real. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. That’s a good question. I, I do think there are a few, but I, I wouldn’t put everything in that bucket.

Residual connections, I still think those are pretty fundamental. If you take them out, it’s really hard to train deep networks. That’s been true for a long time. And you still need some mixing mechanism, self-attention or convolution or something reasonable, and some nonlinearity, feed-forward layers in the right places. That basic skeleton, I, I wouldn’t call a historical accident.

But normalization, yes. That’s a good example of something we inherited. It was there when we figured out how to train these models more stably, and then it just stayed as the default. And what we found with dynamic tanh is you can get a similar kind of squashing behavior without an explicit normalization layer, without collecting mean and variance statistics. So that one, we, we thought was essential, and it turned out more replaceable than people assumed.

Dropout is another one. For a long time people treated it as essential or the model would overfit, and now at the scale we train, a lot of models just don’t use it, or use very little.

And then a lot of the more specific choices, the exact positional encoding, sinusoidal versus learned versus RoPE, the exact activation, GELU, SwiGLU, pre-norm versus post-norm. They matter in the recipe. You have to get them right together with learning rate and the rest of the training setup. But I wouldn’t say any one of them is the core of why the model works. We keep swapping them and we stay on a similar frontier of accuracy versus efficiency.

So the pattern is the same as ConvNeXt, for me. A lot of what we call the identity of the architecture is more historical, more the stack we happened to arrive at. The small details compound, and once the data and the scale and the optimizer change, some of these pieces stop being load-bearing. I still like asking, do we actually need this, or did we just inherit it? Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah. I think, first of all, with normalization, people really believed LayerNorm or RMSNorm was indispensable, right? Like, you couldn't train deep transformers without it because the activations would explode or collapse. But what normalization is really doing is just controlling the scale, controlling the variance of the signal propagation. And what we showed with dynamic tanh is that if you have a proper bounding mechanism on the activations, you don't strictly need normalization layers to train stable, deep networks.

As for other components, I think softmax attention itself is definitely one candidate. People treat the full quadratic softmax self-attention as this sacred, irreplaceable component of modern AI. But as we saw with ConvNeXt, and also with recent works on linear attention or state-space models, if you modernize the rest of the architecture and get the training recipe right, the gap between these different token-mixing mechanisms becomes much smaller than people assume. 

Another one might be positional embeddings—whether it's RoPE, ALiBi, or learned embeddings. People spend a lot of time debating which one is fundamentally better, but as long as the model has some reasonable way to distinguish order and relative distance, it might not be the deciding factor for performance.

So I really do think a lot of these choices are historical accidents. Someone tried something early on, it happened to work, and then the entire community converged on it. And because everyone uses it, all the software, the hardware, the CUDA kernels, and the hyperparameter recipes get optimized around that single choice. Once that happens, it looks like an essential inductive bias, but in reality, it's often just that the alternatives haven't had the same amount of collective engineering poured into them.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a, that's a good question. I think there, there's actually one example that already played out, which is dropout. like if you, if you go back to the papers from, say, ten years ago, dropout was in every network, it was considered, absolutely essential, people would say deep learning doesn't work without, without this regularization. And now we train these giant models with, with basically no dropout at all. So that was something people, considered a core component, and it turned out to be an artifact of the regime we were in, like small data, small models, heavy overfitting. The moment the regime changed, the, the essential component disappeared.

Other things I, I would suspect... positional encoding, maybe. We went from, sinusoidal to learned, to RoPE, and now some people show that NoPE also works. so the particular, the particular form we use today is probably a historical accident, even though having some, some notion of order clearly matters.

And, and I, I would also say the, the whole macro-structure of the block, like attention then feed-forward, then attention then feed-forward, interleaved, nobody ever, really justified that. It just crystallized from, from the original paper. that's why I, I'm happy to see this, this recent work, like the, the hyper-connections style things from these open weight companies, questioning how residual connections are done, how layers connect to each other. Even residual connections, like we treat them as sacred, and I do think they're genuinely important, but the exact way we do them, there may be better, better answers.

and, and tokenization, I think, is a big one. The fact that we discretize language into this fixed vocabulary, is very much an engineering artifact. In the long run, going byte-level or, or continuous, might be more, more natural.

But I, I would hedge here. I think it's, it's very hard to know which components are accidents until someone actually demonstrates an alternative at, at convincing scale, with the same recipe, the same data, properly tuned baselines. and very few claims survive that test. So maybe the, the honest answer is, probably many of them are accidents, but the, the expensive part is proving it. normalization took us years, and, and we got lucky that, that it, it worked out. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah. So, so first I would say, I, I wouldn't call normalization a historical accident exactly. It, it was, it was very useful when it was introduced, right? Batch norm, and then layer norm, they, they really solved a problem at that time. It made training deep networks much easier. So it, it's more like, it was a, a solution for a problem, and then the problem, the community kind of, moved on, we have better initialization, better optimizers, better residual connections, but the component stayed. Nobody, nobody really went back to ask whether we still need it. So in, in that paper, we found that actually what the normalization layer does at, at the end, when you look at the input/output mapping, it's just a, a S-shaped curve, like a tanh. It's, it's squashing the extreme values. So you can just replace it with, a tanh with a learnable scale, and, and it works. So that's, that's the finding. It, it's not that normalization is useless. It's that the, the function it serves can be, achieved by something much simpler.

So to your question, yes, I do think there are other things like that. one that I, I think a lot about is, the softmax in attention. we use softmax because that was the, the natural choice for the, attention weights to be a distribution, but, there's no reason it has to be a probability distribution, right? People have tried, like sigmoid attention, or other, other normalizations there, and it, it can work with the right, with the right details. Another one is, is positional encodings. Like we went from sinusoidal, to learned, to rotary, and each time it's, it's kind of, whatever worked at that scale. I, I'm not sure any of them is, fundamental. and, also things like, weight decay, warmup, the, the learning rate schedule. These are, everybody uses them, but, but I think they, they're mostly, compensating for something else in the, in the training dynamics that we don't fully understand. And tokenization, right? Tokenization is, is very much a, an engineering choice that, that the whole field just, inherited.

But, I, I would say the, the two things I, I'm, I'm more confident are, are essential, are residual connections and, and having some mechanism for tokens to, to communicate, like attention or, or convolution. Everything else, I, I think if you, if you remove it and, and tune everything else carefully, you can, probably recover most of the performance. Yeah. That's, that's kind of my belief, but, I, I could be wrong. Yeah.
